w: Four soaring minarets raised in 1591 as the centrepiece of a brand-new city - climb the stairs and there's still a working mosque on the top floor, in use for over four centuries. Laad Bazaar's bangle stalls crowd its west side, Makkah Masjid its southwest, and Eid crowds still pack the square below.
s: 1591 monument with a mosque still on its top floor
_facts: Monument constructed in 1591, symbol of Hyderabad, on the emblem of Telangana
A mosque has occupied its top floor for more than 434 years
Laad Bazaar lies to the west, Makkah Masjid to the southwest, on the east bank of the Musi River
ASI-listed archaeological and architectural treasure; major Eid gathering site

w: Laid out around the Charminar in 1591 by the city's Qutb Shahi founder, then walled and re-fortified by a Mughal governor in 1712 - most of that wall is gone, but the tangle of lanes it enclosed, from Shah Ali Banda to Moghalpura, is still the symbolic heart of Hyderabad, glass-tower HITEC City notwithstanding.
s: The walled heart Hyderabad grew from, since 1591
_facts: Walled city on the banks of the Musi River, founded 1591 by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah
Fortified in 1712 by Mughal governor Mubariz Khan, completed under the Nizam
Contains neighbourhoods Shah Ali Banda, Yakutpura, Dabirpura, Afzal Gunj, Moghalpura
Remains the symbolic heart of the city alongside HITEC City

w: No donation box, no cash accepted, no fast-track queue for VIPs - a rare Hindu temple that fought a legal battle to stay free of government control, and won. It stands quietly on the banks of Osman Sagar, one of the oldest temples in the old Hyderabad district, run to this day without a single hundi in sight.
s: The temple with no donation box and no VIPs
_facts: Ancient Hindu temple of Lord Balaji on the banks of Osman Sagar
Accepts no money from devotees, has no hundi and no VIP privileges
Fought and won the right to stay out of government control
One of the oldest temples in the historic Hyderabad district

w: A Hanuman shrine that grew into a small pantheon - the main sanctum's Dhyana Anjaneya form is flanked by Rama, Shiva, Durga, Saraswati and others under one roof, near the Nagarjuna Sagar Ring Road. It keeps oddly specific hours, closing for a midday break like an old-fashioned shop before reopening into the evening.
s: A Hanuman shrine that grew into a mini pantheon
_facts: Hindu temple whose presiding deity is Hanuman as Dhyana Anjaneya
Also houses Rama, Shiva, Saraswati, Durga, Santoshimata, Venugopala and Jagannath
Located near Santoshnagar, close to the Nagarjuna Sagar Ring Road
Open 6am-1pm and 4:30-8:30pm daily except Tuesday and Saturday, when hours shift

w: Quiet most of the year, then the centre of attention every summer when the Ghatam procession - devotees carrying painted ceremonial pots - winds through during Bonalu, the folk festival shared by Hyderabad and Secunderabad. A modest Hindu shrine that becomes one of the loudest stages in town for a few colourful days.
s: Quiet shrine, loud stage during Bonalu
_facts: Hindu temple in Hyderabad, popular during the Bonalu festival
Known for its Ghatam procession during Bonalu, celebrated across Hyderabad and Secunderabad

w: A power station's turbines and ash once stood here; by the late 1990s the site had become 36 acres of gardens on the shore of Hussain Sagar, named for the matinee-idol-turned-chief-minister N.T. Rama Rao. It sits amid lakeside attractions - Birla Mandir and Necklace Road an easy stroll away, Lumbini Park next door.
s: Lakeside park built where a power station stood
_facts: 15-hectare park beside Hussain Sagar lake, on the site of a thermal power station that stood until 1995
Named after former Andhra Pradesh chief minister N.T. Rama Rao, built in phases since 1999
Close to Birla Mandir, Necklace Road and Lumbini Park
Maintained by the Buddha Purnima Project Authority

w: A dome of bare rock rising out of the eastern suburbs, topped by a dargah and Shia mosque that give the whole surrounding neighbourhood its name and character. Pilgrims climb the hill year-round, and the area below remains one of the city's few strongly Shia enclaves.
s: A rock dome topped by a dargah and mosque
_facts: Ancient dome-shaped rock hill known for the Moula Ali dargah and a Shia mosque on top
Surrounding area is predominantly inhabited by Shia Muslims

w: Dug in 1897 on the order of the sixth Nizam, this was once Secunderabad's biggest lake and a favourite picnic spot - it has shrunk by more than half since, swallowed acre by acre by illegal building. A 2022 report counted over a thousand encroaching structures, ranking it among the city's most built-over lakes.
s: A Nizam-era lake shrinking under encroachment
_facts: Manmade lake built 1897 by Mahbub Ali Khan, Asaf Jah VI; also called Jeedimetla Cheruvu
Once the largest waterbody in Secunderabad at 290 acres, down to 126 acres by 2014
Popular historic picnic spot
A 2022 report found about 1,014 illegal encroaching structures, ranking it third most encroached in the city

w: Dug in 1626 and left largely clean for three centuries until the city's postwar expansion caught up with it in the 1950s. A 2003 restoration, roughly $2 million of dredging and bank work, brought the water back - and within a few years migratory birds were returning to Saroornagar in numbers again.
s: 1626 lake brought back to life for the birds
_facts: Lake created in 1626, spread over 99 acres, remained clean until the city's expansion in 1956
Restored by the Hyderabad Urban Development Authority in 2003-04 at a cost of about $2.1 million
Migratory birds returned in large numbers a few years after restoration

w: Known locally as the 'Badi Masjid' - the big mosque - this Musheerabad landmark was raised in 1560 by the fourth Qutb Shahi sultan, built as a near-mirror image of the Hayat Bakshi Mosque across town in Hayathnagar. Four and a half centuries on, it's still the neighbourhood's namesake and anchor.
_facts: Also known as Masjid e Kalan or Musheerabad Badi Masjid
Original portion constructed 1560 CE by Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah, fourth Qutb Shahi sultan
Identical in design to the Hayat Bakshi Mosque in Hayathnagar

w: Tucked inside Hyderabad's Public Gardens, next door to the legislative assembly, this mosque was commissioned in 1924 by the last Nizam, Mir Osman Ali Khan, through the City Improvement Board, and finished in 1933 as his own court's principal place of worship. Locals still know it simply as the Public Garden Mosque.
s: The last Nizam's own mosque in the Public Gardens
_facts: Also known as Masjid Awan e Shahi or the Public Garden Mosque, within Hyderabad's Public Gardens
Commissioned 1924 by Nizam Mir Osman Ali Khan, completed 1933
Served as the principal mosque for the seventh Nizam and his courtiers

w: Built in 1518 as the Safa Masjid, before its founder had even declared independence from the Bahmani Sultanate he served - Sultan Quli Qutb Shah commissioned it while still a governor, then went on to found the dynasty that raised Golconda Fort and, decades later, the Charminar itself.
s: 1518 mosque built before the Qutb Shahi dynasty existed
_facts: Friday mosque in Golconda, originally named Safa Masjid
Constructed 1518 CE by Sultan Quli Qutb Shah, then governor of the Bahmani Sultanate, later founder of the Qutb Shahi dynasty

w: An overlooked 16th-century mosque in Ibrahim Bagh, read by historians as the rough draft for the far grander Makkah Masjid downtown - and a leftover fragment of an unfinished Golconda-era city plan. UNESCO added it to a tentative World Heritage list in 2014, still waiting on the wider Deccan Sultanate nomination.
s: The mosque UNESCO calls a Deccan Sultanate draft
_facts: 16th-century mosque built during the reign of Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah, in Ibrahim Bagh
Architectural precursor to the grand Makkah Masjid
Tied to the aborted urban planning of the Golconda Sultanate
Placed on UNESCO's tentative World Heritage list in 2014 under Monuments and Forts of the Deccan Sultanate

w: An 1901 observatory built by a Paigah nobleman and endorsed by the sixth Nizam, kitted out with an 8-inch Cooke astrograph and a 15-inch Grubb refractor. Its astronomers logged over 460,000 star observations for the international Carte du Ciel project, mapping the sky one photographic plate at a time.
_facts: Optical observatory built by Nawab Zafar Jung Bahadur, established by Mahbub Ali Khan, Asaf Jah VI in 1901
Made 463,542 observations for the international Carte du Ciel star-mapping project
Equipped with an 8-inch Cooke Astrograph and a 15-inch Grubb refractor telescope

w: A royal palace on Naubhat Pahad that spent decades reinvented as the Ritz Hotel before passing into state hands as a heritage property. The hilltop setting - chosen for its views over the old city - still gives it an outsized presence over the skyline below.
s: Royal palace turned Ritz Hotel turned heritage site
_facts: Royal palace at Naubhat Pahad, also known as the Ritz Hotel
Now owned by the Government of Telangana / Telangana State Tourism Development Corporation

w: 'Sky House' - built in 1885 by the Paigah noble Sir Asman Jah on a hillock chosen for the view. It has been a palace, a museum of relics, an orphanage and finally a school, each incarnation stripping away a little more of the original: large sections of the INTACH-listed structure were bulldozed by the school in 2021.
s: Palace, museum, orphanage, school - in that order
_facts: Paigah-era palace in Malakpet, built 1885 by Sir Asman Jah; name means 'sky home'
Declared a heritage structure by INTACH; once housed a museum of archaeological relics, later an orphanage
Now a school (St Joseph's Public School), which demolished large parts of the palace in 2021

w: Housed inside the Nizam's own Purani Haveli palace, this small museum is essentially an unwrapped gift pile - the mementos dignitaries sent Osman Ali Khan, the last Nizam, for his 1936 silver jubilee. Among the silverware and curios: miniature silver models of Hyderabad's own landmarks, each labelled in Urdu.
s: A Nizam's silver jubilee gifts, unwrapped for good
_facts: Museum at Purani Haveli palace, showcasing gifts given to the last Nizam Osman Ali Khan for his 1936 silver jubilee
Collection is mainly souvenirs and mementos from dignitaries
Includes silver models of Hyderabad landmarks with Urdu captions
